The Yelling Rescue Tool
The Yelling Rescue

Just yelled?
I got you.

Want to stop yelling?

I got you, too.

A guided reset to help you understand what happened and redesign what happens next.

01 · Before

What actually happened?

Start with the facts. Describe the moment as though a camera recorded it.

Not: “My child was being disrespectful.”

Try: “I asked her to put on her shoes three times and she kept playing.”

What did you make it mean?

Sometimes our body reacts not only to what happened, but to what we believe it means.

02 · What was happening in me?

Where were you before the yell?

You probably didn’t go from 0 → 100. You passed 20… 30… 40… 50…

The goal is not to become superhuman at 100. The goal is to start noticing yourself earlier.

What were you already carrying?

What happened in your body?

03 · What mattered?

What were you actually trying to protect?

Sometimes we get so focused on stopping the conflict that we accidentally remove the thing we actually value.

We are not trying to remove what matters.
We are going to redesign the path to it.
04 · What does my child need?

Is this only a “listening problem”?

Sometimes a boundary needs to be held. And sometimes something else is happening too: your nervous system is reacting to your child while your child may also be reacting to you.

What might your child be responding to?

What might they still need help learning or practicing?

05 · The skill gap

What was missing between KNOWING and DOING?

You may already know what you “should” do. Your child may already know what they “should” do. That does not mean either of you can reliably access that knowledge under pressure.

I may need more skill in…

More skill = more options.
The more options you have, the less pressure you place on willpower.
06 · The redesign

What needs to change before this happens again?

A redesign is not “Next time I’ll try harder.” A redesign changes something practical.

Sometimes you add something. Sometimes you remove something. Sometimes you adjust something already there.

You do not need to do all three. Ask only: What practical change would make this moment easier to lead next time?

Reality check

If you read your redesign tomorrow morning, would you know exactly what to do differently?

Design is not a promise. It is a practical change to the environment, structure, skill, expectation, or support.

07 · Watch me put it into practice

How I redesigned cooking with my kids

I loved the idea of cooking and baking together.

But once the milk spilled, flour went everywhere, and everyone started touching everything… I would go from “Let’s make something fun!” to “STOP! Why are you pouring it like that?!”

What mattered
Cooking, independence, responsibility, and real life skills.
My limitation
Watching the mess happen right beside me made me reactive and controlling.
Skills they needed
Kitchen safety, food safety, following instructions, measuring, cleanup, independence.
My redesign
I taught foundational skills first, gave them boxed cake recipes with prepared instructions and ingredients when they were younger, and stayed close enough to supervise without hovering inside the mess.
The result
Years later, they can cook, bake, clean up, and function independently in a kitchen.
I didn’t remove the value.
I redesigned the path.
08 · The result

What are you actually trying to create?

Your redesign should move you toward something.

09 · Connect the dots

Does your redesign actually lead there?

This is where you self-correct. You are not just choosing a nice-sounding solution. You are testing whether your design logically supports the result you want.

Your redesign
For your child
For you
For the relationship

If you actually make this change, does it reasonably move you toward the result you want?

That’s useful information.
Your design does not have to be perfect on the first try. What needs to change so the redesign better supports the result you want?
10 · Leadership

Decide before the pressure arrives.

Your hardest parenting moment should not be the first time you decide what the boundary is, what matters, what you believe, and how you want to respond.

11 · Self-trust

The goal was never perfect parenting.

It was self-trust.

“I trust myself to lead with what I know, what I have, and everyone’s best interest in mind. And if I get it wrong, I trust myself to repair, learn, and redesign.”
